title: Technical and clinical validation of a novel deep learning-based white matter hyperintensity segmentation tool.
summary: The study trained MD-GRU and nnU-Net deep-learning models for white-matter-hyperintensity segmentation and tested them on datasets excluded from training. Against reference masks and comparator algorithms, the models showed improved agreement, reduced bias and improved repeatability and inter-scanner reproducibility. In the two-year DiViNAS data, nnU-Net yielded a calculated sample size 41% smaller than the best comparator for detecting a treatment effect; this is a statistical-power calculation, not evidence of an observed treatment effect or clinical benefit.
ai_technology: MD-GRU and nnU-Net deep-learning segmentation models for MRI white matter hyperintensities.
organization: Affiliation not stated in the reviewed material

evidence.tested: Technical tests used MarkVCID reference masks and scan-rescan/inter-scanner data plus SWISS-AF images; clinical-biomarker analysis used two-year DiViNAS follow-up. Models improved agreement, bias, precision and reproducibility versus benchmark algorithms; nnU-Net produced a 41% lower calculated sample size than the best comparator for treatment-effect detection.
evidence.unknown: The treatment-effect result is a power calculation from existing follow-up data, not a measured treatment response. The study does not demonstrate improved patient outcomes.
evidence.ai_role: Deep-learning segmentation generates WMH volumes; the resulting measurements were assessed against masks, repeat scans, scanners and longitudinal biomarker data.

source_review.scope: Primary result-bearing material for the stated method, result and evaluation, with bibliographic version information.
